findings.title: containerd CRI plugin: Checkpoint restore bypasses destination security context
findings.summary:
### Impact

A vulnerability in containerd's CRI implementation allows a container restored from an untrusted checkpoint via the `CreateContainer` API to bypass the destination security context and execute with elevated privileges. When restoring a container from a checkpoint archive or annotated OCI image, CRIU restores process credentials, Linux capabilities, `no_new_privs`, and seccomp state directly from checkpoint data rather than enforcing the destination CRI `ContainerConfig`. An attacker who can run a container with a crafted checkpoint image can execute processes as root with full capabilities and no enforced seccomp filters despite restrictive security policies requested by the orchestrator. Additionally, containerd's CRI status reporting reflects the requested configuration rather than the actual restored process state, masking the privilege discrepancy from orchestrators. This issue affects Linux systems running containerd with CRI checkpoint restore enabled; users not utilizing CRI checkpoint restore are not affected.

### Patches

This bug has been addressed in containerd 2.2.7 and 2.3.4 by disabling checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer` by default.  The feature has been removed entirely in containerd 2.4.0. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue. Running containers that were restored from untrusted checkpoints should be stopped, deleted, and recreated.

Users who rely on restore via the `CreateContainer` API can re-enable the feature by setting the new `enable_experimental_restore_via_create` configuration option. However, enabling restore via `CreateContainer` leaves this vulnerability present, as containerd cannot enforce destination security policy during CRIU process restoration. 

### Workarounds

findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. Checking agent outputs with User Alignment Critic The main planning model for Gemini uses page content shared in Chrome to decide what action to take next. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. In this post, we dig into the data behind this shift and also cover: How we’re expanding our reach: We're pushing to make secure code the default across our entire software stack. We have updates on Rust adoption in first-party apps, the Linux kernel, and firmware. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: Claude Code: Plugin Hash Pin Bypass Allows Bypass of Hash Pinning
findings.summary:
The plugin install flow in Claude Code and Claude Desktop checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA using `git checkout` without verifying that the resulting HEAD matched the pinned SHA. An attacker controlling a plugin's upstream repository could create a branch named identically to the pinned 40-character SHA, causing the checkout to silently resolve to the attacker's branch tip instead of the reviewed commit, resulting in attacker-controlled code being installed bypassing the pinned hash. Exploitation required a user to install a malicious plugin, pin to a safe hash, and for the plugin source to be hosted on a git host that permitted SHA-shaped branch names.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix already. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Thank you to Or Nevo Michrowski of Air Security for reporting this issue.

findings.title: kin-openapi: Incomplete Fix for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5: Three Unpatched nil-Items Panic Paths in openapi3filter
Nginx UI: MCP nginx_config_add skips config directive validation → authenticated nginx directive injection (RCE on the official image)
findings.summary:
## Summary
`internal/config/validation.go` (`ValidateConfigFile`) is a security control that blocks dangerous
nginx directives — `js_*`, `perl_*`, `load_module` of the njs/perl modules, and `user root`. It is
enforced on three of the four config-write paths: `api/config/add.go`, `api/config/modify.go`, and
`mcp/config/config_modify.go`. The fourth path — the MCP tool `nginx_config_add`
(`mcp/config/config_add.go`) — does NOT call it: it writes the caller-supplied `content` straight to
disk and reloads nginx. An authenticated MCP caller (or an MCP agent induced via prompt injection)
can therefore inject exactly the directives the control is meant to block, leading to nginx code
execution on deployments where the njs/perl module is available (e.g. the official Docker image).

## Root cause — an incomplete hardening patch
Commit `3e411d38` ("Harden config write paths", 2026-04-21) introduced `ValidateConfigFile` and
wired it into the config-write paths — but its changeset touched only:
  api/config/add.go (+6), api/config/modify.go (+8), internal/config/validation.go (+199),
  mcp/config/config_modify.go (+5)
It did NOT touch `mcp/config/config_add.go`. So the MCP add path was left without the validation
that all of its sibling paths received. `config_add.go` has never called `ValidateConfigFile`
(verified via git history); this is an oversight in the hardening, not a regression.

## Affected code (mcp/config/config_add.go, handleNginxConfigAdd)
```go
content := mcp.GetString(args, "content")        // caller-controlled
...
path, err := config.ResolveConfPath(baseDir, name)   // path is sandboxed to the conf dir (OK)
...
err = os.WriteFile(path, []byte(content), 0644)  // <-- no config.ValidateConfigFile(path, content)
...
res := nginx.Control(nginx.Reload)               // reloads nginx
```
Contrast — the guarded sibling (mcp/config/config_modify.go) does:
```go

if err !=

findings.title: JupyterLab: Command link trust prompt in JupyterLab can trust a document other than the one clicked
findings.summary:
## Description

A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.

Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: `markdownviewer:trust` uses `tracker.currentWidget`, and `notebook:trust` uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.

Users are affected if all of the following are true:

- they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;
- they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;
- they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and
- a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file

### Impact

The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in [GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg).

The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.

findings.title: containerd: Unpack DoS via repeated opaque whiteouts
findings.summary:
### Impact

A vulnerability exists in containerd's layer unpack handler where the processing of certain image layers causes superlinear time complexity. During the unpack operation, specific file configurations within the layer can trigger repeated directory traversals.

Consequently, pulling or importing a maliciously crafted image can result in increased unpack times and a moderate increase in CPU usage. This delays container startup, even if the compressed image layers are small. Additionally, in orchestrators like Kubernetes that apply concurrency limits to image pulls, these excessively long operations can reduce the available concurrency for other pulls, potentially delaying unrelated container deployments.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.5, 2.2.8, 2.0.12, and 1.7.35. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue. Users are advised to only pull and import trusted images from known registries until the patch can be applied.

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank Jakub Ciolek of AlphaSense for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

findings.title: Talos Linux: Support bundle does not redact registry credentials
findings.summary:
### Summary
When generating a support bundle with `talosctl support` the credentials entered for private registries are included in the bundle.


### Details

Within the generated support bundle, inside `resources/registryconfigs.cri.talos.dev.yaml` the `auth` field of the spec is retained.
The same, potentially sensitive information is present within `etcfilespecs.files.talos.dev.yaml`.

### PoC

Simply run `talosctl -n [...] support` on a cluster with a `RegistryAuthConfig` resource 

### Impact

The problem itself is minor, however, anyone who has ever uploaded a support.zip bundle on a github issue, slack thread or public forum could have potentially leaked their internal authentication parameters for a private registry.

In most situations, if the network and credentials are set correctly, this should not be a problem. On the other hand, if the affected registry is publicly accessible, and the provided credentials have write access to it, this could lead to possibly serious consequences, from denial of service, to data loss and possibly existing tag hijacking leading to supply chain compromise, for the affected parties which were under the impression that the support bundle is redacted of sensitive information and thus can be shared publicly.


### Notes

Talos 1.14+ by default encrypts the support bundle to the age recipients specified (defaulting to siderolabs GitHub org members), so the impact is even lower.

### Environment

- Talos version: v1.13.0
- Kubernetes version: 1.35.3
- Platform: amd64

findings.title: KEDA: Privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin via KEDA TriggerAuthentication
findings.summary:
## Summary

A namespace admin who creates a `TriggerAuthentication` and a `ScaledObject` in their own namespace can make the KEDA operator send its own ServiceAccount token to a tenant-controlled URL. That token holds `["*"]/["*"] get` cluster-wide, so it reads every Secret in every namespace, plus `batch/jobs` and `horizontalpodautoscalers` create/delete cluster-wide, `*/scale` update on any workload, `validatingwebhookconfigurations` update (rewrite or disable cluster admission), and `apiservices` update (hijack aggregated API routing). This is effectively privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin in real environments: a cluster-wide Secret read alone is enough to find a token for a more privileged ServiceAccount, and the cluster-wide `batch/jobs` create lets the attacker run a workload in any namespace whose Pod Security Admission level permits it (or that is PSA-exempt, such as `kube-system` , `kyverno`) to reach the node filesystem and a control-plane kubeconfig.

This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-68476: its content filter only requires the loaded file to be a JWT whose subject begins with `system:serviceaccount:`, which the operator's own projected token satisfies by construction. The destination field `hashiCorpVault.address` is unvalidated.

findings.title: kin-openapi spec loader panics on a self-referential additionalProperties $ref (nil-pointer DoS)
findings.summary:
The defect
----------
Confirmed at HEAD (f0407d5, v0.144.0). openapi3/loader.go, inside resolveComponent's drill closure (around line 455), the case *SchemaRef branch for pathPart == "additionalProperties" dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value:

    case *SchemaRef:
        if pathPart == "additionalProperties" {
            if ap := c.Value.AdditionalProperties.Has; ap != nil {   // c.Value can be nil here
                cursor = *ap
            } else {
                cursor = c.Value.AdditionalProperties.Schema
            }
            attempted = true
        }

When a $ref fragment drills through .../additionalProperties of a schema whose Value is still nil (a pure, not-yet-resolved $ref, or a self-reference resolved before its own Value is set), c.Value is nil and the .AdditionalProperties access panics.

Input and attacker
-------------------
A tiny crafted OpenAPI document, one schema, no external refs, no network:

    openapi: 3.0.3
    info: {title: t, version: "1.0.0"}
    paths: {}
    components:

findings.title: Nuxt OG Image cache poisoning through derivable cache keys on unsigned dynamic image routes
findings.summary:
**Vendor:** Nuxt
**Product:** Nuxt OG Image
**Version:** 6.2.5
**Description:** Due to the specifics of caching and key generation in the Open Graph image cache created by the module, an unauthenticated attacker can modify the content of the image (for example, the `title` parameter) that is delivered to the user. 
**Impact:** Content Spoofing
**Vulnerable component:** route `/_og/d/*.png`
**Exploitation conditions:** Access to the application
**Mitigation:** Upgrade to 6.7.2 and set a sufficiently secure `secret` in config `ogImage`
**Researcher:** Dmitry Vanin (Positive Technologies)

## Research
During [the previous vulnerability research](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/og-image/security/advisories/GHSA-6c86-prf5-hj4h), it was discovered that version 6.2.5 changed the mechanism for generating cache indexes; it now takes into account the parameters passed during image generation.

However, the image is still generated from data transmitted to the attacker.

_Listing 1. New code for generating indexes in cache_
```
export function resolvePathCacheKey(e: H3Event, path: string, resolvedOptions?: Record<string, any>) {
  const siteConfig = getSiteConfig(e, {
    resolveRefs: true,
  })
  const basePath = withoutTrailingSlash(withoutLeadingSlash(normalizeKey(path)))
  const hashParts: any[] = [
    basePath,
    import.meta.prerender ? '' : siteConfig.url,
  ]
  // Hash resolved options (not raw query string) so unknown/extra query params
  // cannot produce unique cache keys and bypass the cache.
  if (resolvedOptions)
    hashParts.push(hash(resolvedOptions))
  return [
    (!basePath || basePath === '/') ? 'index' : basePath,
    hash(hashParts),
  ].join(':')
}
```
In this case, `basePath` is obtained from the `_path` parameter, `resolvedOptions` are the normalized settings of the component, for example:

_Listing 2. An example of `resolvedOptions`_
```
{"emojis":"noto","extension":"png","width":1200,"height":600,"cacheMaxAgeSeconds":259200,"component":"OgImageDef

findings.title: OpenNext Cloudflare: Cache interception can bypass middleware protection for encoded paths
findings.summary:
## Summary

When cache interception is enabled, `@opennextjs/cloudflare` can interpret percent-encoded paths differently during middleware matching and cache lookup.

An encoded request may fail to match authorization middleware, then be decoded into the cache key of a protected route. The cached response may consequently be returned without invoking the middleware.

`enableCacheInterception` is disabled by default.

## Impact

A remote unauthenticated attacker may retrieve cached content from routes intended to be protected by middleware.

An application is affected when it:

- explicitly enables `enableCacheInterception`;
- relies on middleware for access control; and
- has a matching cached route.

## Details

Middleware matching previously used the encoded request pathname, while cache interception decoded the pathname before selecting a cache entry.

For example, consider an application with:

- middleware matcher `/admin/:path*`;
- middleware returning `401 Authentication required` for `/admin`;
- a statically generated, cached `/admin` route; and
- cache interception enabled:

```ts
export default defineCloudflareConfig({
  incrementalCache: staticAssetsIncrementalCache,
  enableCacheInterception: true,
});
```

An attacker can request:

```http
GET /%61dmin
```

The encoded pathname does not match `/admin/:path*`, so the authorization middleware is not invoked. Cache interception then decodes `%61dmin` to `admin` and may return the cached `/admin` response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-opennext-cache: HIT

Protected content
```

Malformed paths exposed an additional inconsistency. For example:

```http
GET /%61dmin/%ZZ
```

The previous implementation decoded each segment independently. It decoded `%61dmin` to `admin` but retained the malformed `%ZZ` segment, allowing cache lookup to continue using a partially decoded pathname.

## Patches

findings.title: FrankenPHP: Cross-request PHP session ID leak in worker mode when the session extension is a shared module
findings.summary:
## Summary
In worker mode under concurrency, FrankenPHP can hand a PHP session id from one request to another when PHP's `session` extension is loaded as a shared module instead of being statically linked into the FrankenPHP binary. A request presenting `Cookie: session=A` can have `session_id()` resolve to `B` (a different concurrent client's id) or to a stale id from a previous request served by the same worker thread.

## Impact
- **Security:** cross-user session exposure / session hijacking in worker mode. Same impact class as CVE-2026-24894.
- **Functional:** users are intermittently logged out; their cookie's session is ignored and they receive a foreign or empty session.

## Affected / not affected
Exposure is determined by how the `session` extension is linked in the PHP build FrankenPHP is compiled against, **not** by the FrankenPHP release:

- **Affected:** any build where the `session` extension is not visible to FrankenPHP at compile time, i.e. loaded as a shared / out-of-tree module (`extension=session` in an ini). This includes the RPM and Debian packages and other packaged `php-zts` distributions that ship `session` as a shared extension under `conf.d`.
- **Not affected:** builds where `session` is statically compiled into the PHP that FrankenPHP links against, such as the official static binaries and Docker images. There, the reset code below is compiled in and clears the id every request.

The C session-reset code is unchanged across 1.11.x-1.12.x, so this is not a code regression between releases. A "1.12.2 works / 1.12.3 leaks" observation on the same host reflects two differently-built packages, not a source change. The persistent-zval helpers (#2366) are compiled only under `FRANKENPHP_TEST` and are unrelated.

## Root cause
FrankenPHP resets per-request session state in `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`, which releases `PS(id)` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie. That whole function is guarded by `#ifdef HAVE_PHP_SESSION

findings.title: Nginx UI: OTP secure-session step-up can be bypassed via MCP configuration tools
findings.summary:
### Summary
An OTP-enabled authenticated user who cannot use the HTTP configuration mutation endpoints without a valid secure session can still mutate Nginx configuration through `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` using only ordinary authentication.

### Details
The HTTP configuration mutation surface is explicitly grouped behind `middleware.RequireSecureSession()`. By contrast, the MCP endpoints are exposed with only `middleware.AuthRequired()`. The MCP server exposes configuration mutation tools including `nginx_config_add` and `nginx_config_modify`, so OTP-enabled users gain an alternate path around the intended step-up requirement.

Relevant code paths:
- [api/config/router.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/api/config/router.go:14)
- [internal/middleware/secure_session.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/middleware/secure_session.go:52)
- [mcp/router.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/router.go:9)
- [mcp/config/config_add.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/config/config_add.go:34)
- [mcp/config/config_modify.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/config/config_modify.go:55)

This is a security-control bypass rather than a missing feature. The product already established that OTP-enabled users should complete a secure session before high-impact configuration mutations are accepted on the HTTP path.

### PoC
I verified this locally in an isolated environment with a temporary end-to-end harness that exercised the real `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` routes.

What the executed test did:
1. Created a temporary config directory and configured Nginx control commands to harmless local values (`true`) to avoid touching the host.
2. Created a real OTP-enabled user in a temporary SQLite database.
3. Generated a real JWT for that OTP-enabled user.
4. Started a local test server exposing the real `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` routes.
5. Opened an authenticated SSE connection to `/mcp` with the JWT and no `X-Secure-Session-ID`.
6. Initialized the MCP session

findings.title: Nginx UI: MCP `nginx_config_add` Bypasses Directive Validation — Authenticated RCE
findings.summary:
### Summary

The MCP tool `nginx_config_add` writes nginx configuration files to disk and triggers an nginx reload without calling `config.ValidateConfigFile`. The identical flow in the REST API (`POST /api/configs`) does call that function and correctly rejects dangerous directives. An authenticated attacker can exploit this gap to write config files containing any blocked directive (`perl`, `js_import`, `load_module`, `user root`, etc.), bypassing nginx-ui's entire security layer. On a server with the nginx Perl, njs, or Lua module loaded, this is post-authentication Remote Code Execution.

### Details

`api/config/add.go` (line 46) calls `config.ValidateConfigFile` before writing:

```go
err = config.ValidateConfigFile(path, content)  // validates directives, checks blocklist
if err != nil {
    cosy.ErrHandler(c, err)
    return
}
```

`mcp/config/config_add.go` (line 79) omits that call entirely and writes directly:

```go
err = os.WriteFile(path, []byte(content), 0644)  // no ValidateConfigFile, no blocklist check
...
res := nginx.Control(nginx.Reload)               // reload triggered immediately
```

`config.ValidateConfigFile` runs two checks:
- **`ValidateConfigContent`** — rejects control characters, enforces encoding.
- **`ValidateConfigDirectives`** — rejects a blocklist of dangerous directives: `perl`, `perl_modules`, `perl_require`, `perl_set`, `js_import`, `js_set`, `js_content`, `load_module` (restricted modules), `user root`, and others.

Neither check runs on the MCP path. Note that `mcp/config/config_modify.go` does call `ValidateConfigFile` correctly — only `config_add.go` is affected.

The MCP endpoint (`GET /mcp` SSE + `POST /mcp_message` JSON-RPC) accepts the same JWT and node-secret tokens as the REST API, so the attack surface is any authenticated session.

**1 — Control: confirm REST API blocks the payload**

{ "name": "rce.conf", "base_dir": "conf.d", "content": "<perl config below>",

findings.title: Nginx UI: Auto backup name allows path traversal outside validated storage path
findings.summary:
## Summary

Nginx UI validates `backup_path` and `storage_path` against the administrator-defined `backup.GrantedAccessPath` boundary, but the final auto-backup output filename is built from the user-controlled auto-backup `name` without stripping path separators or `..` components.

An authenticated user who can create or modify an auto-backup task can set a name such as `task/../../../escaped`. The configured `storage_path` still passes validation because it is inside `GrantedAccessPath`, but the generated backup path escapes that storage directory when `filepath.Join(storage_path, filename)` resolves the embedded traversal sequence.

This bypasses the documented backup path boundary and allows backup archives, and for encrypted configuration backups the adjacent `.key` file, to be written outside the intended storage directory with the Nginx UI process privileges.

## Affected Versions

- Current `dev` branch commit checked: `4948fba8744e82c3d7003f68ee164e9f49421066`
- Latest release checked: `v2.3.10`, published 2026-04-28
- The vulnerable filename construction is present in both current `dev` and `v2.3.10`.

## Security Boundary

The project documentation describes `backup.GrantedAccessPath` as the critical security boundary for backup operations. It says the setting:

- restricts backup operations to explicitly authorized directories,
- prevents unauthorized access to sensitive system directories,
- enforces administrator-defined boundaries,
- normalizes paths to prevent traversal attempts.

That boundary is enforced for the configured `storage_path`, but not for the final path after the backup name is appended.

## Root Cause

`model.AutoBackup.GetName()` only trims whitespace and replaces spaces:

```go
func (a *AutoBackup) GetName() string {
    return strings.ReplaceAll(strings.TrimSpace(a.Name), " ", "_")
}
```

The result is then embedded directly into filenames:

```go
filename := fmt.Sprintf("%s_%d.zip", autoBackup.GetName(), time.Now().Unix())
outputP

findings.title: Junrar: RarVM VM_JMP maxOpCount bypass causes infinite CPU loop during RAR4 extraction
GitHub CLI allows path traversal through unescaped request URL components
findings.summary:
### Summary

A path traversal vulnerability has been identified in the GitHub CLI where some HTTP request URLs, REST API calls in particular, were built without properly escaping their variable path components. A value containing URL path metacharacters can alter the request path and cause `gh` to address a different resource than intended.

### Details

Not all request URLs in the codebase were built with proper escaping of their variable path components. When a component is interpolated into the path without percent encoding, and that component contains URL path metacharacters, it breaks out of its intended segment and changes the effective request path.

In `2.97.0`, request URLs are constructed in a safe manner, so a variable component can no longer escape its intended segment.

### Impact

An attacker who can control a value that flows into a request path can cause `gh` to send the request to a different API endpoint than intended. This can lead the CLI to read or act on a resource other than the one the user meant to target.

### Remediation and Mitigation

1. Upgrade `gh` to `2.97.0`.
2. Be cautious when running `gh` against untrusted repositories or inputs whose names you do not control.

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ).
